notes: Access: plain direct HTTP fetch, no WAF/bot-block. Found Clearance nested under Sale in the site's own taxonomy: the /sale/ page's embedded category-tree JSON contains {"id":"cat930424","name":"Clearance", ... "pageTitle":"Clearance | Cookware, Bakeware, Kitchen Tools", "parentCategoryTree":[{"id":"cat2211269","name":"Sale"},{"id":"cat930424","name":"Clearance"}]} - i.e. Clearance is a genuine, permanently-named taxonomy node (not a temporary campaign), satisfying the Clearance-vs-Sale test even though it lives under the /sale/ URL path. Its canonical URL is https://www.surlatable.com/sale/clearance-2/ (react-helmet title 'Clearance | Cookware, Bakeware, Kitchen Tools | Sur La Table'). Three other sitemap URLs - /sale/clearance-1/, /clearance-2/, and /extra-20%25-off-clearance/ - were verified (curl -L) to be 301 redirects to this same canonical page, so they are aliases and not recorded as separate rows. The taxonomy node reports "onlineSubCategoriesCount":5, matching the 5 department sub-pages found in the sitemap under /sale/clearance/<dept>/ (linens, coffee-tea, bakeware, everyday-entertaining, tools) - every one of these was fetched and each shows '0 Items' (or a generic placeholder 'Category Search' template with no products), i.e. the genuine sub-structure currently exists but is empty, so per the zero-product rule none of the 5 are recorded as rows. EXCLUDED as generic/promotional Sale, not Clearance, per the brief's core test: /sale/ itself ('Sur La Table Sales & Special Offers'), /sale/sur-la-table-sale/*, /sale/all-sale/, /sale/under-*, /cyber-monday/*, /holidays/thanksgiving/flash-sale/, *-sale/ department pages (cookware-sale, bakeware-sale, etc.), /sale/19.72-specials/, /sale/buy-2-get-1-free-tools-*, /sale/limited-time-offers/, /sale/second-servings-resale-marketplace/ (a resale marketplace concept, not clearance) - all are temporary/seasonal promotional campaigns with no permanence signal in the site's own taxonomy. Site search was not used since robots.txt disallows /search*; the embedded taxonomy JSON was direct, stronger evidence anyway.
